For anyone who still doesn't completely get the theme, Jim Horne at xwordinfo.com sums it up in a neat chart:

Theme entry	Comparative reading
LITTERBUG	A firefly is a "litter bug"—more lit than a fruit fly.
OLIVER STONE	Peridot is an "oliver stone"—more olive-colored than jade.
BUTCHER BLOCK	Muscle Beach is a "butcher block"—a more butch stretch of beachfront.
LIGHTER FLUID	Oil is a lighter fluid than water.
SHUTTERFLY	A zipped-up zipper makes for a "shutter fly"—more shut.
BUFFER ZONE	The weight room is a "buffer zone"—associated with buffer people than the cardio room.
EASTER ISLAND	Maui is an "easter island"—farther east than Oahu.
BOMBER JACKET	A blazer is a "bomber jacket"—more bomb, or stylish, than a windbreaker.
SOONER STATE	Delaware became a state sooner than the other original colonies.
HYPERTEXT	The exuberant message is "hyper text"—more hype, treating that slang word as an adjective.

A little tongue-in-cheek advice to aspiring or already aspired constructors: don’t collaborate with John Kugelman. The hate is just going to rub off on you, and any credit for the zaniness and inspired chaos (if there is any) is just going to him.

If there’s a more stereotypically Kuglemanesque puzzle out there I can’t remember it. I’m beginning to resonate with Matt’s comment the last Kugelman collaboration. I feel dirty. I feel like an enabler. I feel like we all, solvers and editors alike, let John get away with this because we all sit back and allow it.

Seriously, this was just groaner after groaner and in the end I loved it. But I have a warped brain. I don’t want to dwell on the clues—not too hard, thank God, because the theme was the star and I just had to get through it as fast as possible before my brain exploded. (Alas I had to flyspeck YASIR/YASAR/FERRATE/FERRITE—luckily duct tape was handy.) I won’t even mention those odd little clues that only Kugelman comes  up with, which again I weirdly enjoy.

Oh, my favorite theme answers were the ones with silly improper comparative adjectives, such as LITTER instead of “more lit”, SHUTTER instead of “more shut”, and EASTER instead of “more east”.

The answer set – how did they come up with these?  There is not only silliness, but there’s wit, and I’m guessing plenty of hard work behind creating this theme set. Several of these theme answers gave me jaw-drop smiles.   

Sure, my brain enjoyed some areas of resistance, with slippery cluing, and it had a great time trying to come up with the theme answers with as few crosses as possible, which I didn’t find easy. 

But, Dylan and John, give me silly that makes me smile, and I’m on your side for the whole puzzle.  And you did, and I was.  And that, to me, was the best part of this puzzle.  This was a hoot and most satisfying.  Please consider pairing again, and thank you!

I would like to say something intelligent about magnetism.

And by that I mean, I wish I were intellectually capable of doing so.  

Alas.

Magnetism has always baffled me.  There are few things about magnetism I'm (mostly) sure of.  

Like electric fields and magnetic fields are inextricably linked.  Shame there's not one more, and it could serve as the Trinity.

But I digress.  

It occurs to me that when we think about electricity, we think about little balls with an electrical charge moving around.  But we (or at least I) don't have such an image with a magnetic field.

That seems wrong to me--if electricity and magnetism are forever interlocked, why would we think about them so differently?  Is it because we're not thinking correctly about either of them?

One last thing.   Spinning, charged atomic objects produce a magnetic field.  We are surrounded by an enormous number of extremely powerful magnets, which, together could create a magnetic field of staggering intensity.

But they don't, because almost every one of those magnets is in alignment with another magnet to cancel out the field.  What's left is the tiny magnetic field we use for compasses.

Or so I think.  But I warned you--I'm no good at magnetism.

As for the cross, Yasar, though far less common than Yasir as an Arabic name for prosperity is nonetheless an Arabic man's name for prosperity. 
As stated by AI on a Google query---

Is "Yasar" Used as a Name in Arab Countries?

• As a First Name: Using Yasar (يسار) as a given first name in Arab countries is rare compared to Yasir. When parents do choose it, it is typically for its secondary vocabulary meaning of "abundance, ease, prosperity, wealth" rather than "left-handed."
• As a Last Name: It is much more common to find Yasar used as a family name (surname) across the Middle East.

Apparently, Yasir/Yasar can also be spelled "Yasser" when transliterated, as in Yasser Arafat.

Boy, was I slow today!  Some of the puns I didn't fully get until I had seen many more of them.  The first one, LITTER BUG, was a great big "Huh?"  I got BUG of course, but why LITTER?

I understood it when I got to the marvelous SHUTTER FLY.  A "more shut" FLY!.. Yesss!!!  So that means the firefly LITTER BUG is a "more lit" bug.  Got it!  It's all so wonderful!  The LIGHTER FLUID and the OLIVER STONE and the BUFFER ZONE and the SOONER STATE!  So clever and imaginative and different!  While I usually reserve my POY nominations to completely new puzzle theme-types -- and pun-type Sundays are hardly new -- few pun-type Sundays have ever been this good.  So into my POY list it goes.

Nor will you be bored working the non-theme parts of the puzzle.  There are few names and very little mindless trivia.  Most of the answers are vocabulary-based, interestingly clued, and require thinking.

Really enjoyed this one a lot!  And I bet Dylan and John had a great deal of fun making it.  Their joy in the creative process is palpable.
